strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: adapting frozen CLIP retrievers to shifted query distributions without costly re-embedding and redeployment of vector indexes, a concern that is real at industrial scale.

The 'score inflation' phenomenon under similarity-based rewards is a genuine and interesting finding. The analysis (Fig. 5, Fig. 6) showing similarity rising while Recall@1 falls, driven by generic high-frequency tokens, is convincing and provides real insight into why naive similarity rewards fail.

Comprehensive evaluation across three CLIP backbones (ViT-B/32, B/16, L/14) and five benchmarks covering multilingual, length, and modality shifts, with consistent gains (+4.5% R@1, +4.9% R@10 on average over the frozen-LLM rewriting baseline).
Data-efficiency ablation (Fig. 4) showing 88-94% of full performance with 10k samples is useful for practitioners.
Good limitations discussion: the paper honestly identifies the dependence on LLM knowledge coverage (per-language analysis in Fig. 7), the retriever upper bound, and inference latency costs.
Appendix provides prompt templates, training details, and dataset statistics, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Missing key baselines weaken the central claim. The paper only compares GRPO with ranking reward vs. GRPO with similarity reward. Crucially absent are: (i) supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of the rewriter on strong rewrites or ground-truth captions, (ii) simple non-RL pipelines (translation + query expansion, prompt-ensemble rewriting), and (iii) alternative RL algorithms (e.g., PPO, REINFORCE). Without these, it is unclear whether GRPO specifically, or merely any rank-aware finetuning signal, drives the gains.

The 'plug-and-play, no retraining' framing is somewhat overstated. GRAPE requires per-dataset RL finetuning on that dataset's training split, using ground-truth target rankings as reward. This is a supervised training cost (though cheaper than re-embedding), and the method inherits the labeled-data requirement that training-free baselines do not have. The paper should more clearly acknowledge this trade-off.

The 'theoretical analysis' (Appendix A.1) is a routine two-line computation showing GRPO's group-normalized advantage is affine-invariant. Presenting this as a derivation justifying the reward design overstates its contribution; it shows any monotone linear map of ranks is equivalent, but does not establish that rank-based rewards are superior to similarity rewards.

No statistical significance testing, error bars, or multiple seeds are reported. Given GRPO training variance and the modest margins on some benchmarks (e.g., CIRR R@1: 35.7 vs 30.7 for ViT-B/16, but 33.2 vs 29.7 for ViT-L/14 with similar LLM baseline variability), single-run results are hard to assess.

Some experimental setup details are confusing or under-specified: XM3600 has 33,218 validation queries against only 456 validation images; the Wikipedia dataset (Rasiwasia et al., 2010) is described only vaguely; the choice of K rewrites per query is not stated in the main text; and Figure 1's advantage computation (mean 1.2, std 0.4 with rewards 2.0, -5.5, ...) appears numerically inconsistent.
Inference-time cost of rewriting every query with an LLM is acknowledged as a limitation but never quantified (latency, throughput), which matters for the deployment story that motivates the paper.

Presentation issues: the code URL in the abstract is blank; several grammatical errors ('more effective... and bridge the distributional shifts', 'explicitly recover latent entities'); acronym 'GPRO' appears in the title where 'GRPO' is presumably intended—a conspicuous error in the paper's title.

Novelty is incremental: it is a straightforward application of GRPO to query rewriting with a linear rank-based reward; the reward (Eq. 4) and format reward are standard components, and RL-based query rewriting/reranking exists in prior IR literature, which is not thoroughly discussed.

strengths: The practical motivation is genuine: adapting queries rather than re-embedding billions of vectors is a real deployment concern for frozen CLIP-based retrieval systems.

The empirical observation of 'score inflation' under similarity-based rewards (Fig. 5 and Fig. 6: similarity rises while Recall@1 falls) is a nice, concrete failure-mode finding that is well-motivated and illustrated.

The evaluation spans multiple distribution shifts (multilingual, long-form, compositional) and three CLIP backbones, and includes data-efficiency ablations and per-language analysis on XM3600 in the appendix.
The appendix provides a clean affine-invariance argument explaining why the normalized advantage depends only on ranking order, giving theoretical grounding for the reward choice.
Limitations are discussed honestly (LLM knowledge coverage bounds gains, retriever upper bound, inference latency).
weaknesses: The core framing is inconsistent with the method's actual requirements. GRAPE needs labeled query–target pairs from the downstream dataset (the reward is the rank of the ground-truth target image) and is finetuned per benchmark on that dataset's training split. This is essentially per-task supervised RL finetuning, which undercuts the central 'no supervision / distribution shift / plug-and-play' narrative. If gold pairs exist at training time, the obvious and critical missing baseline is supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of the rewriter on those same pairs (e.g., using human translations/gold captions), whose absence makes the headline gains over 'CLIP+LLM' uninterpretable.

Novelty is limited: the method is GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) applied to query rewriting with a rank-based reward. RL for query rewriting/reformulation with retrieval feedback exists in the RAG/search literature, and this line of work is not discussed; the reward design in Eq. 4 is a simple linear rank mapping. The claimed corpus-relative ranking idea amounts to standard GRPO group normalization over a rank reward.

The comparison to prior art is weak. The only baselines are vanilla CLIP and a frozen-LLM rewriter; no prior training-free or RL-based rewriting methods (e.g., variants of PlugIR, ComCLIP-style decomposition, or any published query-rewriting system) are quantitatively compared. The 4.9% average gain is only over the authors' own +LLM baseline.

Some baseline cells are simply unavailable ('—' for CLIP on Flickr30k-CN and CIRR), so for several datasets the paper never establishes how far the system is from a meaningful CLIP reference, and CIRR uses a different, larger rewriter (Qwen2-VL-7B) than the other datasets (Qwen2.5-3B), confounding the cross-dataset comparison.

Evaluation corpora are very small (e.g., 1,000 validation images for Flickr30k-CN, 693 for Wikipedia, 456 for XM3600 val), which limits the practical relevance of R@1/R@10 numbers for the large-scale retrieval deployments the paper motivates; no analysis of how rewards and performance scale with corpus size N, even though the reward in Eq. 4 is defined over N candidates.

Reproducibility is undermined: the abstract states 'The code is available at' followed by nothing, no variance or statistical significance is reported for any result, and GRPO training details (e.g., number of rollouts beyond batch size 8, exact candidate-pool construction for ranking during training) are incomplete.

Presentation issues: the title contains a typo ('GPRO'), the method section headings and text are inconsistent (Section 2.2 describes GRAPE under 'Training-Free Retrieval' despite it requiring per-dataset RL training), the advantage formula in Section 3.2 is garbled, and key terms like 'corpus-relative' are used loosely without a precise definition of the candidate set.

The score-inflation analysis, while interesting, is only demonstrated on one dataset/backbone combination and is not connected quantitatively to the final results; the claim that ranking rewards 'suppress' inflation is asserted more than rigorously tested across settings.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely practical problem: improving frozen CLIP retrievers without re-embedding or redeployment, which is a real deployment constraint at industrial scale.

The score-inflation phenomenon with similarity-based rewards is an interesting and non-obvious empirical finding, and it is convincingly demonstrated both qualitatively (Fig. 5 rewritten-query examples showing generic-token exploitation) and quantitatively (similarity rises while R@1 falls; Fig. 6 comparison).

Evaluations are reasonably broad: five benchmarks spanning three kinds of distribution shift (multilingual, length, modality), three CLIP backbones, and consistent gains (~4.5% R@1, ~4.9% R@10 over the frozen-LLM baseline).
The data-efficiency analysis (Fig. 4) shows most of the gain is achievable with ~10% of training data, which strengthens the practical value of the method.

The limitations section is honest and specific: dependence on LLM knowledge coverage (illustrated with per-language XM3600 results), the retriever's intrinsic upper bound, and added inference latency.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core contribution is applying GRPO with a linearly rank-mapped reward to query rewriting. The affine-invariance 'proof' in Appendix A.1 is a trivial two-line computation and does not constitute a meaningful theoretical contribution; the reward itself (Eq. 4) is standard.

A critical baseline is missing: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of the rewriter on ground-truth rewrites or distillation from a stronger teacher. Without it, it is unclear how much of the gain comes specifically from ranking-based RL versus any per-task adaptation of the rewriter. The only ablation against an alternative reward (similarity) is relegated to the appendix on a single dataset (Flickr30k-CN, ViT-B/16).

The CLIP+LLM comparison is arguably unfair: GRAPE is trained on the training split of each target dataset (requiring labeled ground-truth targets), while the baseline is a frozen LLM with a hand-written prompt. Some gains may stem from task adaptation or prompt/format optimization rather than the ranking reward per se; an ablation with GRPO plus a format-only or random reward would clarify this. This also tempers the 'plug-and-play' claim, since the method still requires labeled training data per downstream task.

No variance reporting, error bars, or significance tests anywhere, despite relatively small margins on some benchmarks (e.g., CIRR R@10 is identical between +LLM and +GRAPE for ViT-B/16; CVLUE R@1 gains are ~1-2 points).

The Wikipedia dataset (Rasiwasia et al., 2010) description and citation appear mismatched — Rasiwasia et al. is a cross-modal multimedia retrieval paper, not a Wikipedia long-query benchmark — raising concerns about experimental documentation quality. The paper also frequently cites arXiv preprints for works that are published (e.g., AltCLIP, LLM2CLIP).

Reproducibility is incomplete: the code link in the abstract is literally truncated ('The code is available at'), and key details such as group size K, lambda in Eq. 3, and number of candidate images N used during reward computation are not specified in the main text.

The multimodal (CIRR) setting changes both the rewriter model (Qwen2-VL-7B vs. Qwen2.5-3B) and the task, making cross-benchmark comparisons harder to interpret; discussion of this design choice is thin.

Discussion of inference cost is qualitative only ('the extra cost is modest'); no latency or token-throughput numbers are given, despite this being a headline motivation for the frozen-retriever design.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: improving frozen-CLIP retrieval under distributional shifts (multilingual, long-form, multimodal queries) without retraining the retriever or re-embedding the corpus. The motivation and positioning relative to training-based vs. training-free methods are clear.

The 'score inflation' phenomenon (Figures 5-6) is a genuinely interesting empirical finding: supervising rewrites with absolute similarity can monotonically increase target similarity while degrading Recall@1, driven by non-discriminative generic tokens. The corpus-relative ranking reward is a simple, well-motivated fix, and the appendix analysis (shared-mean decomposition, affine invariance of the GRPO advantage, variance stability) gives a reasonable intuition for why ranking rewards are more robust.

The evaluation is unusually broad for this line of work: five benchmarks spanning three shift types, three CLIP backbones (ViT-B/32, B/16, L/14), data-efficiency curves (Figure 4), group-size sensitivity (Table 6), comparison against training-free baselines including proprietary LLMs and PlugIR (Table 4), and per-language analysis on XM3600 (Figure 7).

The limitations discussion is honest and substantive: LLM knowledge bottleneck (with per-language evidence), retriever-dependent performance ceiling, and inference latency are all explicitly acknowledged rather than buried.

Case studies (Figures 2-3) concretely illustrate the behavioral differences between vanilla LLM rewrites and GRAPE rewrites, supporting the qualitative claims about translation enrichment, distillation, and cross-modal grounding.
weaknesses: A critical baseline is missing: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of the same rewriter LLM on the same training data. The paper repeatedly contrasts GRAPE with 'conventional SFT' (Section 4.4) but never actually runs an SFT rewriter (e.g., trained on gold captions as target rewrites). Without this, it is impossible to attribute the gains specifically to the ranking-based RL objective rather than to any finetuning of the rewriter. This directly weakens the paper's central claim that ranking-aware GRPO supervision is the key ingredient.

The vanilla CLIP baseline is absent (dashes) for Flickr30k-CN, CVLUE, and CIRR in Table 1, so the headline improvements over the true baseline cannot be verified on three of five benchmarks; effectively all comparisons are against CLIP+LLM zero-shot rewriting, and the average gain (~4.5% R@1 / 4.9% R@10) is modest. Several cells show essentially no gain (e.g., CIRR R@10 for ViT-B/16 is identical at 77.8), suggesting the benefit is not uniformly consistent.

No variance or statistical significance is reported: single runs, no seeds, no confidence intervals, despite the improvements being only a few points and GRPO training with LLMs being notoriously high-variance. Claims of 'consistency' would be more credible with repeated runs.

Reproducibility gaps: the abstract states 'The code is available at' with no URL; several experimental details are ambiguous (e.g., Table 4 evaluates on 'Flickr-CN (1k)' without explaining the subset; Table 2 statistics look puzzling, e.g., XM3600 with 126,341 train queries but only 1,745 train images and 33,218 val queries vs. 456 val images, which is inconsistent with the published XM3600 corpus and needs explanation).

A few reporting details raise concerns: the baseline model names in Table 4 ('Claude-Sonnet-4.6', 'GPT-5.4') are non-standard and should be precisely identified with versions/dates; the Wikipedia dataset is cited to Rasiwasia et al. (2010), which is a cross-modal multimedia dataset rather than an obvious source of long-form Wikipedia queries, so the data provenance for this benchmark needs clarification.

The theoretical analysis in Appendix A.1 is somewhat superficial: the z = mu + z-tilde decomposition assumes a single shared corpus mean, which is a strong simplification of real embedding geometry, and the 'affine invariance' observation largely restates a property of GRPO's normalization rather than proving a benefit of the specific reward.

Generalization is under-tested: the rewriter is finetuned per-dataset on in-domain training sets. The practically compelling scenario for the 'plug-and-play' framing would be a rewriter trained once and transferred to unseen domains/retrievers; cross-dataset or cross-retriever transfer is not evaluated (the three CLIP backbones share text-side limitations, and the text encoder changes across variants, yet per-backbone training setups are not disentangled).

strengths: The paper addresses a practically motivated problem: adapting CLIP-based retrieval to distributional shifts (multilingual, long-form, multimodal queries) without retraining the retriever or re-embedding the corpus, which is genuinely relevant to deployed industrial systems.

The identified 'score inflation' phenomenon—where similarity-based supervision teaches the rewriter to inject generic, non-discriminative tokens that raise absolute similarity but degrade ranking—is an interesting and empirically supported observation (Fig. 5 and Fig. 6 show similarity rising while Recall@1 collapses under similarity rewards).

The proposed ranking-based reward (Eq. 4) is a simple, sensible fix that directly aligns the RL objective with the evaluation metric, and the paper includes several useful ablations: data-efficiency sweeps (Fig. 4), group-size sensitivity (Table 6), length-characterization on Wikipedia (Table 5), and per-language analysis on XM3600 (Fig. 7).
The limitations discussion is relatively honest (LLM knowledge bottleneck, retriever-dependent ceiling, inference latency), and the impact statement addresses potential bias amplification.
The method keeps the retriever and corpus embeddings frozen, which strengthens the plug-and-play deployment claim.
weaknesses: Critical baseline rows are missing in Table 1: the vanilla CLIP baseline is shown as '—' for Flickr30k-CN, CVLUE, and CIRR across all model scales. This makes it impossible to verify the total headroom that LLM rewriting and GRAPE actually provide, and weakens the central claim that GRAPE 'consistently improves performance'; the reader can only assess gains over CLIP+LLM, not over the raw system.

The reported dataset statistics raise serious concerns about evaluation validity: XM3600 is presented with 126,341 train queries but only 1,745 train images and a 33,218-query validation set over 456 images. XM3600 is an evaluation-only benchmark (~3,600 images, 36 languages); the provenance of this enormous train/val split is unexplained, and training a per-dataset GRPO policy on splits of an evaluation benchmark risks contamination and inflates results. Similarly, training on the training split of each test benchmark (rather than a separate corpus) limits claims about generalization.

The baseline comparison in Table 4 cites 'GPT-5.4' and 'Claude-Sonnet-4.6' as proprietary baselines. These model names do not correspond to any verifiable released systems, which severely undermines the credibility of that comparison and of the paper's reporting overall.

No statistical rigor: results are single-run point estimates without variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests, despite the modest average margin (+4.9% R@10) being the headline claim; several per-cell gains are within plausible seed noise.

The theoretical analysis in Appendix A.1 is largely trivial: the affine-invariance of group-normalized advantages is a known property of GRPO-style normalization rather than a new contribution, and the 'score inflation' decomposition (z = μ + z̃) is heuristic rather than a formal result.

Inconsistent experimental setup across tasks: the CIRR experiments use Qwen2-VL-7B while all other benchmarks use Qwen2.5-3B, confounding comparisons of modality-shift gains against length/language gains.

The abstract states 'The code is available at' with no actual link, which harms reproducibility, and key hyperparameters (λ, clip thresholds, candidate pool size N, number of retrieved items at reward computation) are deferred or unspecified in the main text.

Missing comparisons to obvious stronger baselines, e.g., SFT of the rewriter on gold caption/query pairs, or supervised prompt optimization, would clarify whether GRPO is necessary versus cheaper supervised alternatives.

strengths: Clear and practical motivation: improving frozen CLIP retrievers under distribution shift (multilingual, long-form, multimodal) without retraining the retriever or re-embedding the corpus addresses a genuine deployment pain point.

The core finding of 'score inflation' under similarity-based supervision is interesting and well-supported: Figure 5/6 show similarity rising while Recall@1 degrades, and Appendix A.1 gives a plausible theoretical account (the shared corpus-mean term q^T mu cancels under ranking) plus an affine-invariance argument for why ranking rewards stabilize GRPO normalization.

Broad empirical coverage: five benchmarks spanning three shift types, three CLIP backbones (ViT-B/32, B/16, L/14), data-efficiency ablations, group-size sensitivity, comparison against PlugIR and strong proprietary LLM rewriters (GPT-5.4, Claude-Sonnet), and a manual failure-mode audit (14% -> 3% failure rate).

Case studies (Figures 2 and 3) concretely illustrate the qualitative behavior GRAPE learns (entity recovery, distillation of long text, cross-modal integration), aiding understanding of why the method works.
Honest limitations discussion covering the LLM knowledge bottleneck, retriever-dependent performance ceiling, and inference latency overhead, plus per-language analysis showing where gains shrink.
weaknesses: Evaluation protocol raises comparability and leakage concerns: the train/validation splits in Table 2 are non-standard for several benchmarks (e.g., XM3600 is a 3,600-image evaluation set yet is reported with 126k train queries and 1,745 train images; Wikipedia with 2,173 train pairs). GRPO is trained per-dataset on that dataset's training split and then evaluated on a custom validation split, making results hard to compare with prior published numbers and raising the possibility that training-set ranking supervision leaks dataset-specific statistics into evaluation.

The headline 4.9% R@10 gain is measured against the authors' own CLIP+LLM baseline, not against the best available alternatives. There is no comparison with strong training-based methods that the paper itself cites (Long-CLIP, LoTLIP, LLM2CLIP) on the same benchmarks, so the practical significance relative to simply adopting a stronger retriever remains unquantified. The baseline CLIP numbers are also absent ('--') for several benchmarks, obscuring how much gain comes from LLM rewriting alone versus GRPO.

No variance reporting: all results appear to be single runs without seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests, despite RL finetuning being notoriously high-variance; several margins (e.g., CVLUE ViT-B/32 13.1 vs 12.1 R@1) are small.

Reproducibility is undermined: the code link in the abstract is empty ('The code is available at'), and key hyperparameters (number of GRPO steps per dataset, reward weighting between format and ranking reward, KL coefficient lambda) are deferred or only partially specified.

A potential circularity in the reward is not fully analyzed: the ranking reward uses the rank of the ground-truth target image during training, so the policy is optimized directly on the evaluation objective; the paper would benefit from analysis of out-of-distribution rewriting (train on one benchmark, test on another) to demonstrate the learned behavior generalizes rather than overfits.

The deployed benefit claim ('no re-embedding needed') comes at the cost of an LLM forward pass on every query, which the paper acknowledges; quantitative latency measurements are missing, weakening the practicality argument.
